title: How Big Is the Universe, Really? The Scale Will Break Your Brain
description: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across, even though the universe itself is only 13.8 billion years old. Starting in our own solar system, this film walks outward one scale at a time, through the nearest stars, our galaxy, the local cluster, and finally to the true edge of what light lets us see, and asks what might lie beyond it.

beats.say: The universe you can see is about 93 billion light-years across. The universe itself is only about 13.8 billion years old. On the surface, that should be impossible.

Light cannot cross a gap that wide in that little time, so how are you able to see all of it? The answer is that space itself has been stretching this whole time, and it carried that ancient light along with it.

To understand how something can be both that young and that vast, start small, right here in your own solar system, and work outward, one leap at a time, past planets, past stars, past entire galaxies, all the way to the edge of what light lets you see.
Earth orbits the sun at a distance of about 150 million kilometers. Even at the speed of light, that gap takes over 8 minutes to cross.
Keep moving outward and the distances jump fast. Mars sits roughly 225 million kilometers from the sun, and Jupiter, the largest planet, is nearly 780 million kilometers out.
Pluto, out at the edge of the known planets, orbits about 5.9 billion kilometers from the sun, so far that sunlight needs more than 5 hours to arrive there.
Beyond Pluto lies the Kuiper Belt, a vast ring of icy bodies stretching for billions more kilometers before the sun's influence finally fades into interstellar space.

The farthest human-made object ever launched, a small spacecraft called Voyager 1, lifted off in 1977 and has been flying outward ever since. It only crossed into interstellar space in 2012, after 35 years of travel.

And even after nearly 50 years of nonstop travel at tens of thousands of kilometers per hour, Voyager 1 is still nowhere near the next star. To measure that kind of distance, you need a completely different unit.
Light travels at about 300,000 kilometers every second, fast enough to circle the entire Earth 7 times before you finish blinking.
In one year, light covers about 9.5 trillion kilometers. Astronomers call that distance a light-year, and out here, it is the only unit that makes sense.
Using that unit, the nearest star beyond our sun, a small red star called Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.2 light-years away.
That means the light reaching your eyes from it tonight left more than 4 years ago. With today's fastest spacecraft, actually traveling there would take tens of thousands of years.
On the clearest night, away from city lights, you can see roughly 9,000 stars with the naked eye. Every single one lies inside our own galaxy, and most are far closer than the galaxy's true edge.
And Proxima Centauri is just one neighbor. Your sun is only one of hundreds of billions of stars inside a single galaxy.
The Milky Way, your home galaxy, stretches about 100,000 light-years from one edge to the other. Crossing it at the speed of light would still take 100,000 years.
It holds somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars, arranged in a flat spinning disk with great spiral arms curling out from the center.
Your solar system sits roughly halfway out from that center, orbiting the galaxy's core once every 230 million years or so.
The last time your solar system was in this exact spot in its orbit, dinosaurs had not yet appeared on Earth.
At the very center of the Milky Way sits a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*, with a mass more than 4 million times that of the sun.
And the Milky Way itself, as huge as it is, turns out to be just one galaxy among an almost unimaginable number of others.

The nearest large galaxy to ours is Andromeda, roughly 2.5 million light-years away. Its light left it long before modern humans existed, yet you can still spot it with nothing but your own eyes on a clear, dark night.
The Milky Way, Andromeda, and around 80 smaller galaxies together form what astronomers simply call the Local Group.
Even that neighborhood is small on the largest scales. Groups of galaxies gather into clusters, and clusters gather into superclusters, some stretching hundreds of millions of light-years across.
Our own Local Group sits on the outer edge of one such structure, the Virgo Supercluster, itself just a thread inside something even bigger.
The Virgo Cluster alone, the dense heart of our supercluster, contains more than 1,000 galaxies bound together by gravity.
Zoom out far enough, and galaxies stop looking scattered at all. They trace out a vast, web-like structure, with great empty voids stretched between the strands.

chapters.title: The Edge of What We Can See

beats.say: Current surveys put the number of galaxies in the observable universe at roughly 2 trillion, and most of them are too far away for their light to have ever reached Earth.

stat.label: estimated galaxies in the observable universe

beats.say: That limit exists because the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so light from anything farther than 13.8 billion light-years has simply not had time to get here yet.

You would expect the observable universe to be about 13.8 billion light-years across then, a simple one-to-one match between age and size. For a universe that was not expanding, that would be exactly correct.
But while that ancient light was traveling toward you, space itself kept expanding, stretching the distance between here and wherever that light first began.
That stretching is why the observable universe now measures about 93 billion light-years across, nearly 7 times wider than its age alone would suggest.
That leftover light is not only sitting in visible galaxies, either. The very oldest light of all does not come from stars at all. It comes from the universe's own afterglow.
That oldest light is called the cosmic microwave background, and it comes from an era when the universe was only about 380,000 years old, far too young for a single star to have formed yet.

stat.label: age of the universe when this light was released

beats.say: Before that point, the universe was so hot and dense that light could not travel freely at all. It scattered constantly, the way light scatters inside thick fog.
As the universe cooled and expanded, that fog finally cleared, and light was set free to travel in every direction for the first time. Some of it is still arriving today.
Scientists discovered it completely by accident in 1965, picking up a faint, even hiss of radio noise coming from every direction in the sky at once.
That faint glow is the oldest light anyone has ever detected, a direct baby picture of the universe taken when it was only a small fraction of its current age.
That 93-billion-light-year sphere is not a wall or a boundary in space. It is simply the farthest distance light has managed to reach you since the universe began.
Scientists have measured the large-scale shape of space itself and found no sign of an edge, and no sign that it curves back on itself.

Some cosmologists have proposed the universe could loop back on itself like the surface of a sphere, so that traveling far enough in one direction would bring you back to where you started. So far, precise measurements have found no evidence of any such curve.
That means the full universe is very likely larger than the part you can observe, and it may be far larger, or it may even go on forever.
Nobody can prove that either way, because no signal, not even light, can travel fast enough to show us what lies beyond the part we can already see.
Right now, in every direction, space keeps stretching outward into a distance that no human alive will ever measure or map.

So here's the question for you: if the universe really does go on forever, with no edge and no center, does that change how you think about your own place inside it? Type your answer in the comments below.
